scenes.name: 1a Cold open: 1921
scenes.text: December, nineteen twenty-one. On the edge of Tunis, a local official named Paul [Gielly](/ʒiˈɛli/) notices a man on his hands and knees in the moonlight, prising carved stones out of the ground.

scenes.name: 1b Urns
scenes.text: What lay beneath those stones would become one of the most argued-over sites in archaeology: urn after urn of burnt bones. The bones of babies, and of young lambs.

scenes.name: 1c Two teams
scenes.text: Two teams of scientists have since studied the same remains. They reached conflicting conclusions.

scenes.name: 1d The question
scenes.text: Were these children offered to the gods? Or mourned, and given a burial of their own?

scenes.name: 2a From Tyre to Carthage
scenes.text: Carthage was a Phoenician city, linked to the great port of Tyre, some two thousand three hundred kilometres to the east. Tradition names its founder as a princess of Tyre: [Elissa](/ɪlˈɪsə/), better known as Dido.

scenes.name: 2b Gulf of Tunis
scenes.text: It stood on the Gulf of Tunis, in what is now Tunisia.

scenes.name: 2c Rise and fall
scenes.text: From the sixth century BC it grew into a trading power whose reach spanned much of the Mediterranean, until Rome destroyed it in one hundred and forty-six BC.

scenes.name: 2d The tophet
scenes.text: Close to its ancient harbours lies an open-air sacred precinct. Archaeologists call it the [tophet](/tˈəʊfɛt/). It is the same word the Hebrew Bible uses for a condemned place of child burning near Jerusalem.

scenes.name: 3b One season
scenes.text: The first excavators moved fast. In a single season in nineteen twenty-five, an expedition led by Francis Kelsey lifted out around a thousand urns, recording little about where each one lay.

scenes.name: 3a Excavations
scenes.text: It took until the nineteen-seventies, and an international campaign to save ancient Carthage, for a team led by the American archaeologist Lawrence Stager to dig the precinct layer by layer.

scenes.name: 3c Six centuries
scenes.text: In a trench of roughly a hundred and fifty square metres they recovered hundreds of urns, buried over some six centuries, from around the eighth century BC until the city fell.

scenes.name: 3d Contents
scenes.text: Inside were the cremated remains of very young infants. Some urns held only animals: mostly young lambs, a few birds. Some held an infant and a lamb together.

scenes.name: 3e Amulets
scenes.text: And in about three in ten of the urns studied, someone had placed small amulets. They were only ever with human remains, and only after the fire.

scenes.name: 4a Diodorus
scenes.text: Long before any excavation, Carthage already had a reputation. Writing in the first century BC, the Greek historian [Diodorus](/daɪədˈɔːɹəs/) [Siculus](/sˈɪkjʊləs/) described a siege in three hundred and ten BC. He claimed that the Carthaginians, fearing their gods had turned against them, sacrificed two hundred children of their noblest families to a god he called Cronus.

scenes.name: 4b Plutarch
scenes.text: Later, the Greek writer Plutarch wrote of parents offering their own children, and of mothers forbidden to weep.

scenes.name: 4c Outsiders
scenes.text: But these are accusations by outsiders: Greek authors, not Carthaginians. And [Diodorus](/daɪədˈɔːɹəs/) wrote more than two centuries after the siege he describes.

scenes.name: 4d Supposed eye-witnesses
scenes.text: Jeffrey Schwartz's team points out that the sacrifice interpretation rests partly on accounts like these, which they call supposed eye-witness reports.

scenes.name: 4e Not proof
scenes.text: Hostile sources are not necessarily false. But on their own, they are not proof.

scenes.name: 5a Voices in stone
scenes.text: The Carthaginians themselves left something different: stone. Above many urns stand carved markers. Their inscriptions, in the Punic language, record a vow to the goddess [Tanit](/tˈɑːniːt/) and the god [Ba'al](/bˈɑːəl/) [Hammon](/hɑmˈəʊn/),

scenes.name: 5b The vow formula
scenes.text: and often a reason: because the god heard his voice, and blessed him.

scenes.name: 5c Promised gifts
scenes.text: For Lawrence Stager, that wording was crucial. These were promised gifts, given after a prayer was answered. That, he argued, is hard to reconcile with an infant who had already died.

scenes.name: 5d mlk
scenes.text: A few inscriptions use a word, [molk](/mˈɒlk/). Following the scholar Otto [Eissfeldt](/ˈaɪsfɛlt/), many researchers, including Paolo [Xella](/ksˈɛlə/), read it as the name of a kind of sacrificial offering, not a god called [Moloch](/mˈəʊlɒk/).

scenes.name: 5e The priest stela
scenes.text: Even the carvings divide experts. One stela shows a priest holding an infant. Stager saw a living child, about to be offered. Schwartz's team see an infant who has already died.

scenes.name: 6a Age is the key
scenes.text: Which brings us to the bones themselves. Cremated infant bones are tiny, fragile, and distorted by fire. To estimate age at death, specialists measure fragments of the skull and hip, and examine developing teeth. The case for or against sacrifice depends largely on those ages.

scenes.name: 6b Neonatal line
scenes.text: One clue is a faint line in the tooth enamel, called the neonatal line. It forms only if a baby survives at least a week or two after birth.

scenes.name: 6c Shrinkage
scenes.text: But fire shrinks bone. It may damage the enamel too.

scenes.name: 6d Correction matters
scenes.text: How much you correct for that changes the answer.

scenes.name: 7a Two verdicts
scenes.text: Jeffrey Schwartz and his colleagues studied cremated remains from three hundred and forty-eight urns from the nineteen-seventies excavation. In their twenty seventeen summary, about a quarter of the individuals were prenatal, and many more died around birth, or within the first month. They found the neonatal line in twenty-four of the fifty individuals they sampled. To them, that pattern matches natural infant mortality in an ancient city. The tophet, they argue, was a burial place for those who died shortly before or after birth, whatever the cause, though they accept the Carthaginians may occasionally have sacrificed humans. Patricia Smith's team examined largely the same collection. Correcting for shrinkage, and arguing that cremation can erase the neonatal line, they concluded that most of the infants died at one to one and a half months: past birth, and in their view unlike an ordinary infant cemetery. To them, sacrifice was very probable.

scenes.name: 7b Same bones
scenes.text: Same bones. Two verdicts. In exchanges running from twenty ten to twenty seventeen, each team argued in print that the other had made mistakes.

scenes.name: 8a Beyond Carthage
scenes.text: Carthage was not alone. Precincts like this appear across the central Mediterranean, in North Africa, Sardinia, Sicily, and perhaps Malta. Yet no convincing example has been found in the Phoenician homeland itself. Paolo [Xella](/ksˈɛlə/) argues the custom still came from the east, probably from Tyre. The question remains open.

scenes.name: 8b Zita
scenes.text: At [Zita](/zˈiːtə/), in southern Tunisia, a tophet used after Carthage fell, researchers studying twelve cremated children found signs of hard lives and illness, and of careful burial. They found no concrete sign of sacrifice, but could not say whether the precinct was a cemetery, a place of sacrifice, or both.

scenes.name: 8c New excavations
scenes.text: And at Carthage, Tunisian-led excavations since twenty fourteen are dating the precinct's layers more precisely than ever before.

scenes.name: 9a Shows / cannot show
scenes.text: So what can the evidence establish? That for some six centuries, people here cremated infants and young animals, and buried them with care, under stones carved with vows. That their enemies accused them of child sacrifice. What it cannot yet establish is how each of these children died.

scenes.name: 9b Uncertain as ever
scenes.text: In twenty twenty-four, one independent review of the newest research concluded that the interpretation of the tophet remains as uncertain as ever.

scenes.name: 10a Two stories
scenes.text: A hundred years after that night in nineteen twenty-one, the urns have been excavated, the bones measured, the inscriptions read. And still, the evidence leaves two stories standing: children offered to the gods, or children mourned, and buried with care.

scenes.name: 10b The ground
scenes.text: Perhaps the most honest thing archaeology can say is the hardest to hear. We don't know yet. But the answer may still be there, in the ground beneath Carthage.
